[Logistic Regression III]{.custom-title}




[Grayson White]{.custom-subtitle} [Stat 243
Fall 2026, Week 11]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Recall: Donner Party ::::: columns ::: {.column .center width="55%" .nonincremental} - Two brothers, George and Jacob decide to leave Illinois and lead a group of migrants to head west to California. - Expected trip duration: **four to six months** - Slowed by taking a new route, the Hastings Cutoff, which crossed the Wasatch mountains and Great Salt Lake Desert. - In early **November**, the "Donner Party" is trapped by an early snowfall in the Sierra Nevada mountains. ::: ::: {.column .center width="45%"} ![](img/donner.webp){width="80%"} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Data: Donner Party ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(Sleuth3) data(case2001) donner <- case2001 %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(Survived = case_when( Status == "Survived" ~ 1, Status == "Died" ~ 0 )) donner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 4 Age Sex Status Survived 1 23 Male Died 0 2 40 Female Survived 1 3 40 Male Survived 1 4 30 Male Died 0 5 28 Male Died 0 6 40 Male Died 0 7 45 Female Died 0 8 62 Male Died 0 9 65 Male Died 0 10 45 Female Died 0 # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: :::
What does a row represent? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Exploratory data analysis ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = donner, mapping = aes(x = Sex, fill = Status)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Exploratory data analysis ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = donner, mapping = aes(x = Age, y = Status, color = Sex)) + geom_boxplot(color = "black", alpha = 0.5) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Logistic Regression Logistic regression can be used when: **Response variable**: A **categorical** variable with **two** categories ```{=tex} \begin{align*} Y = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \mbox{success} \\ 0 & \mbox{failure} \\ \end{array} \right. \end{align*} ``` ::: fragment $Y \sim$ Bernoulli$(p)$ where $p = P(Y = 1) = P(\mbox{success})$. ::: ::: fragment **Explanatory variables**: Can be a mix of categorical and quantitative ::: ::: fragment **Goal**: Build a model for $P(Y = 1)$. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why can't we use linear regression? :::: {columns} ::: {.column} - Regression line = estimated **probability** of success - For valid values of $x$, we are predicting the probability is less than 0 or greater than 1. ::: ::: {.column .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why can't we use linear regression? :::: {columns} ::: {.column .nonincremental} - Regression line = estimated **probability** of success - For valid values of $x$, we are predicting the probability is less than 0 or greater than 1. - The estimated probabilities based on the logistic regression model are bounded between 0 and 1. ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: fragment What does the **logistic regression model** look like? ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Logistic Regression Model ```{=tex} \begin{align*} \log\left(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1 - P(Y = 1)} \right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p \end{align*} ``` ::: fragment Left hand side has many interpretations: ```{=tex} \begin{align*} \mbox{LHS} &= \log\left(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1 - P(Y = 1)} \right)\\ &= \log \left( \mbox{odds (of success)} \right)\\ &= \mbox{logit}(P(Y = 1)) \end{align*} ``` Note: $$ \mbox{odds} = \frac{\mbox{prob of success}}{\mbox{prob of failure}} $$ ::: # **Question**: How do we fit the model (the red curve) in R? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Logistic Regression Model in `R` Instead of a **linear** regression model, let's fit a **logistic** regression model to the Donner Party data! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(broom) mod <- glm(Survived ~ Sex + Age + Sex*Age, data = donner, family = "binomial") tidy(mod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 7.25 3.21 2.26 0.0238 2 SexMale -6.93 3.40 -2.04 0.0415 3 Age -0.194 0.0874 -2.22 0.0264 4 SexMale:Age 0.162 0.0943 1.71 0.0865 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Fitted model: $$ \log\left(\frac{P(Y = 1)}{1 - P(Y = 1)} \right) = 7.25 - 6.93 x_{Sex:Male} - 0.19 x_{Age} + 0.16 x_{SexMale:Age} $$ ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Plotting our model ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(donner, aes(x = Age, y = Survived, color = Sex)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 3) + labs(y = "P(Y = 1)") + geom_smooth(method = 'glm', method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction How can I use this model to predict, for a given sex and age: (1) the odds of survival, (2) the probability of survival, and (3) whether or not we expect survival? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction How can I use this model to predict, for a given sex and age: ::: {.nonincremental} (1) **the odds of survival**, (2) the probability of survival, and (3) whether or not we expect survival? $$ \text{odds} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{1 - P(Y = 1)} = \exp\left(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x_1 + \hat\beta_2x_2 + \hat\beta_3x_1 x_2\right) $$ ::: {.fragment} In `R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} odds <- exp( predict(mod, newdata = data.frame(Age = c(20, 65), Sex = c("Female", "Male"))) ) odds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 28.9306659 0.1665121 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction How can I use this model to predict, for a given sex and age: ::: {.nonincremental} (1) the odds of survival, (2) **the probability of survival**, and (3) whether or not we expect survival? :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(donner, aes(x = Age, y = Survived, color = Sex)) + geom_point(size = 3) + labs(y = "P(Y = 1)") + geom_smooth(method = 'glm', method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction How can I use this model to predict, for a given sex and age: ::: {.nonincremental} (1) the odds of survival, (2) **the probability of survival**, and (3) whether or not we expect survival? :::
:::: {.nonincremental .columns} ::: {.column} $$ P(Y = 1) = \frac{\exp\left(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x_1 + \hat\beta_2x_2 + \hat\beta_3x_1 x_2\right)}{1 + \left(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x_1 + \hat\beta_2x_2 + \hat\beta_3x_1 x_2\right)} $$ ::: ::: {.column .fragment} In `R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob <- odds / (1 + odds) prob ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 0.9665895 0.1427436 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # or prob <- predict(mod, newdata = data.frame(Age = c(20, 65), Sex = c("Female", "Male")), type = "response") prob ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 0.9665895 0.1427436 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction How can I use this model to predict, for a given sex and age: ::: {.nonincremental} (1) the odds of survival, (2) the probability of survival, and (3) **whether or not we expect survival**? ::: We can use the **predicted probability** at for an individual to help us predict the **binary outcome**. $$\widehat{P(Y = 1)} \geq 0.5 \rightarrow \hat{y} = 1$$ $$\widehat{P(Y = 1)} < 0.5 \rightarrow \hat{y} = 0$$ ::: {.fragment} In `R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob >= 0.5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Predicted probability of survival for each member of the Donner Party ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} preds <- predict(mod, newdata = donner, type = "response") head(preds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 4 5 6 0.3944507 0.3736522 0.2727419 0.3416426 0.3563990 0.2727419 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Prediction Accuracy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} donner %>% bind_cols(preds = preds) %>% # quickly add as a column mutate(pred_survived = case_when( preds >= 0.5 ~ 1, preds < 0.5 ~ 0 )) %>% group_by(Survived) %>% count(pred_survived) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 # Groups: Survived [2] Survived pred_survived n 1 0 0 24 2 0 1 1 3 1 0 11 4 1 1 9 ``` ::: ::: - Pretty good! - How should we quantify our error rates? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Confusion Matrix Let's see how well our model performs on the training data! - First, obtain predictions for `Survived` based on model and 0.5 cutoff: ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} probs <- predict(mod, newdata = donner, type = "response") preds <- ifelse(probs >= 0.5, 1, 0) ``` ::: ::: - Second, create a **confusion matrix** between `preds` and `truth`: ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} truth <- donner$Survived table(preds, truth) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth preds 0 1 0 24 11 1 1 9 ``` ::: ::: e.g., there were 11 members of the Donner Party who *survived* that we predicted would *not* survive. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Error Measures Recall the **Mean Zero-One Loss** or **Error Rate** is the proportion of incorrect classifications: $$ \textrm{MZOL} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(y_i \neq \hat{y}_i) $$ - `accuracy()` function from `yardstick` returns proportion of *correct* predictions: ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(yardstick) results <- data.frame(truth = factor(truth), preds = factor(preds), probs) accuracy(results, truth = truth, estimate = preds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 accuracy binary 0.733 ``` ::: ::: ::: - To obtain the mean zero-one loss / error rate, we can subtract our accuracy from 1: ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} acc <- accuracy(results, truth = truth, estimate = preds)$.estimate 1 - acc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2666667 ``` ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Changing the Classification Cut-off The *classic* classification procedure chooses the most likely class according to the model: $$ \hat{Y} = \begin{cases} 1,& \textrm{ if } p(X) \geq 0.5,\\ 0,& \textrm{ if } p(X) < 0.5 \end{cases} $$ ::: fragment But we can change the cut-off of 0.5 to: $$ \hat{Y} = \begin{cases} 1,& \textrm{ if } p(X) \geq c_0,\\ 0,& \textrm{ if } p(X) < c_0 \end{cases} $$ for some new cut-off $c_0$ between 0 and 1. ::: - **Q:** What are implications of choosing $c_0 < 0.5$? [Easier to predict $\hat{Y}=1$]{.fragment} - **Q:** What are implications of choosing $c_0 > 0.5$? [Harder to predict $\hat{Y}=1$]{.fragment} - **Q:** Why might we change our cut-off? [To control types of errors!]{.fragment} ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Sensitivity and Specificity For a given classification cut-off, - **Sensitivity:** Proportion of *"successes"* ($Y=1$, survived) correctly classified - **Specificity:** Proportion of *"failures"* ($Y=0$, died) correctly classified
::: fragment By: - *decreasing* the classification cut-off, we *increase* sensitivity and *reduce* specificity - *increasing* the classification cut-off, we *reduce* sensitivity and *increase* specificity :::
::: fragment [How do we choose a cut-off to best **balance this trade-off?**]{style="color: tomato;"} ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curves **ROC curves** plot Sensitivity vs. (1 - Specificity), based on classification probabilities. ::: nonincremental - **Sensitivity:** Proportion of *"successes"* ($Y=1$) correctly classified as $\hat{Y} = 1$ - **(1 - Specificity):** Proportion of *"failures"* ($Y=0$) [incorrectly]{.underline} classified as $\hat{Y} = 1$ - Cutoff $c_0$ is decreasing as we move from left to right. ::: :::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: fragment **Q:** What does the ROC curve look like for a perfectly accurate model? ::: ::: fragment - Straight line up, then across :::
::: fragment **Q:** What does the "kink" in the ROC curve correspond to? ::: ::: fragment - Value of $c_0$ when sensitivity stops improving as much ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ROC Curves in R The `roc_curve` function in the `yardstick` package can create ROC curves. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} r <- roc_curve(data = results, truth = truth, probs, event_level = "second") autoplot(r) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk11fri_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ROC Curves in R What is the ideal cutoff, $c_0$? - Generally, $c_0$ corresponding to "kink" in the ROC curve. - i.e., $c_0$ for which ROC curve is closest to point $(0,1)$ ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} r$distance <- sqrt((0 - (1 - r$specificity))^2 + (1 - r$sensitivity)^2) r %>% arrange(distance) %>% head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 4 .threshold specificity sensitivity distance 1 0.394 0.84 0.6 0.431 2 0.387 0.8 0.6 0.447 3 0.418 0.92 0.55 0.457 4 0.374 0.6 0.7 0.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} best_c0 <- r %>% arrange(distance) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(.threshold) ``` ::: ::: ::: fragment **"Kink" Cut-off = 0.3945** ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Confusion Matrices, Compared Let's compare confusion matrices based on $c_0 = 0.5$ vs. $c_0 = 0.3945$
:::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} **$c_0 = 0.5$** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} preds_05 <- ifelse(probs >= 0.5, 1, 0) table(preds = preds_05, truth) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth preds 0 1 0 24 11 1 1 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} **$c_0 = 0.3945$** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} preds_best <- ifelse(probs >= best_c0, 1, 0) table(preds = preds_best, truth) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` truth preds 0 1 0 21 8 1 4 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: fragment
Comparing error rates ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 cutoff error_rate sensitivity specificity 1 0.5 0.267 0.45 0.96 2 0.394 0.267 0.6 0.84 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Logistic and Linear Regression as **Generalized Linear Models** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Next time - We'll dive deeper into the logistic regression model and linear regression model as **generalized linear models**
